title: Do evolving agents use their senses to find food?
question: Three environment-shift tests failed their manipulation checks: swapping left and right (N, N3) or swapping the food and hazard channels (exploratory pilot, 4 seeds) did not lower the foraging of fixed-wiring agents. A probe of two evolved populations (8000 ticks, about 6 generations, no learning) found innate food and hazard weights near the founder value (about 1.2) with no left/right structure. If evolved wiring ignores sensory information, those shifts could not matter, and the innate-foraging gain in E (+5.5) must come from something other than sensing, such as moving more. This study scrambles the food and hazard sensors and asks whether foraging depends on them.
background: Intervention: scramble_senses=True shuffles the 6 food/hazard sensor values every tick with a dedicated random stream. The total input current is unchanged, but which value comes from which direction and object is lost. Hunger and social sensors are untouched. sense_gain is the innate-foraging assay (each of up to 8 surviving genomes alone in a fresh world for 300 ticks, learning off, as in E) with real senses minus the same genomes with scrambled senses. Positive-control pilot (exploratory, not registered): single agents trained for 40 episodes ate 4.03 food per test episode with real senses vs 2.60 scrambled (6 training seeds x 16 test worlds; lower in 5/6), so scrambling removes information a trained agent uses. In the same pilot untrained random wiring ate 1.0 with real senses vs 2.5 scrambled. Interpretation rule, fixed in advance: if H36a and H36b are both not supported, foraging in evolving populations does not measurably depend on sensory information, and earlier interpretations that assume sensory-guided innate foraging (E, N, N3) must be re-read. Seeds 2000-2011 have never been run.

hypotheses.statement: Evolved innate wiring uses the senses: its genomes forage better with real than with scrambled senses (no-learning populations)
Evolving populations without learning eat more with real senses than with scrambled senses
Evolving populations with learning eat more with real senses than with scrambled senses
Evolving with real senses yields more sense use than evolving with scrambled senses (no learning)
